title: Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents
summary: Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents Alignment Science Blog Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents Alex Remedios 1* , Simon Storf 1* October 22, 2026 Fabien Roger 2 , John Hughes 2 1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 Anthropic * Primary contributors. Name order randomised. tl;dr We red-team production blocking monitors (Auto Mode in Claude Code, Guardian in OpenAI’s Codex) with an adversarial agent in an experimental setting with the objective of improving the safety of coding agents. Our most effective attack strategies bypass the monitor using agent-generated prompt injection against the monitor, multi-agent attacks, or malicious compaction. We attempt to improve the robustness of auto-mode by improving tool coverage, transcript formatting and using an agentic monitor stage. We find that robustly preventing multi-context attacks at an acceptable cost remains an open problem. 📝 Paper , 💻 Code Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program . Introduction Coding agents can now run for days with little or no human involvement, completing software tasks end to end ( Kwa et al., 2025 ). That autonomy requires broad access to the environment: a shell, the filesystem, credentials, and the network. title: オントロジーを基盤に、意思決定・実行を支援するAIエージェントプラットフォーム「Sakana Aquarium」
summary: Sakana AIは、オントロジーを基盤に組織の意思決定とその実行を支援するAIエージェント構築・実行・運用プラットフォーム「Sakana Aquarium（以下、Aquarium）」を発表しました。 Aquariumは、組織に合わせたAIエージェントを効率的に構築し、安全に運用し続けるためのプラットフォームです。散らばる情報をオントロジーで共通の定義に整理し、その上でAIエージェントが情報の確認から判断、実行までを担います。 詳細は、 Aquariumのプラットフォーム紹介ページ をご覧ください。 Aquariumとは 何を根拠に、どのような手順で判断するかは、組織ごとに異なります。Aquariumは、こうした組織固有の判断の前提をAIが扱える形に整え、その上でAIエージェントを動かすためのプラットフォームです。中核となるのは、次の3つの仕組みです。 Ontology（オントロジー） ：組織の判断を支える知識・ルール・データを、それぞれの意味や相互の関係とともに体系化します。テーブルや文書など形式の異なる情報を、既存の保存先から移し替えることなくつなぎ、更新も反映するため、AIエージェントは最新の状況をもとに判断できます。 Governance（ガバナンス） ：データ・オントロジー・エージェントを統制します。アクセス権限や実行前の承認を設定し、判断の根拠から実行結果までを記録します。実行の速度・精度やモデルの利用状況も把握できます。 Managed Agents（エージェント実行基盤） ：オントロジー上の情報をもとに、AIエージェントがタスクを実行します。情報の参照、AIによる判断、関数の実行、人の承認をワークフローとして記述するだけでデプロイでき、エージェントのライフサイクル全体を管理します。 整備したデータとオントロジーは別のエージェントでもそのまま使えるため、オペレーションごとのエージェントを素早く立ち上げ、同じ基盤でまとめて管理できます。多くの魚がひとつの水槽で整えられた環境のもとに泳ぐ姿になぞらえ、「Aquarium（水族館）」と名付けました。 Aquariumで変わる組織の判断と行動 Aquariumが目指すのは、組織に蓄積された情報を、日々の判断と行動に活かせるようにすることです。一度整備したデータの接続とオントロジーは別のエージェントでもそのまま使えるため、AIの活用を組織の中で広げやすくなります。 組織のあらゆる情報を、意思決定に。 組織に蓄積されたデータや文書をAIが読み取り、幅広い情報を判断の材料にできます。 状況の変化を捉え、迅速な対応へ。 更新された情報をもとに状況を把握できるため、各所から情報を集め直す負担が減り、判断と対応に集中できます。 人の関与の下、AIが機敏に実行。 定められた権限とルールのもとで、AIが情報の確認から実行までを担い、必要な箇所で人が承認します。 判断の根拠をたどり、オペレーションを改善。 AIが参照した情報、判断、承認、実行結果を記録からたどり、手順の見直しにつなげられます。 AIソリューション構築の、これまでとこれから Sakana AIは設立以来、 推論時スケーリング や複数モデルの協調、 自己改善 など、モデルを大きくすること以外の方法でAIの能力を引き上げる研究に取り組んできました。並行して、金融をはじめ精度と説明責任が求められる領域で、AIの実装を重ねてきました（三菱UFJ銀行との AI融資エキスパート 、SMBCグループとの 提案書自動生成 、大和証券グループとの 共同開発 など

title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems
summary: For three weeks, from July 21st to August 11th, 1 a METR employee and a Redwood Research employee conducted a pilot high-access exercise to stress-test OpenAI’s internal misalignment monitoring system. 2 The output of this exercise was a 61-page internal report that was shared with OpenAI researchers and security staff, 3 primarily focused on estimating the fraction of agentic inference that is monitored, and whether agents could in principle disable or subvert the monitoring system. The exercise focused on the internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st, and did not evaluate changes that were in progress at the time of the exercise. This exercise involved a deep level of access. The METR and Redwood employees had access to OpenAI’s internal codebase, misalignment-monitor prompts / configuration details, and internal documentation, and conducted technical interviews with approximately a dozen researchers and engineers across the monitoring, safety-systems, and security teams. To enable this level of access, they worked on OpenAI-issued devices, which never left the premises, and were accompanied while onsite. METR, Redwood Research, and OpenAI designed this exercise as a pilot for giving external researchers deep access to internal infrastructure, not to provide robust public transparency about OpenAI’s monitoring systems. 4 As a result, we agreed upfront with OpenAI that we would only publish a relatively brief and high-level public post. title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
summary: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval). Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
summary: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host. title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models
summary: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.

title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
summary: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
summary: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation News today from Anthropic: We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). I'm pleased to note I called this one last December , when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard": I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF , recently the new home of the MCP specification. Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to " Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body ".
